questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Select a craft material to suit the function of an object.
questions.prompt: A class needs a freestanding name card for each craft table. Each card must hold its folded shape without a separate stand. Which material is most suitable?
questions.answer: Light card from a clean cereal carton.
questions.explanation: Light card takes a crease and is stiff enough to stand when folded into a tent shape.
options: Loose dry sand.
Light card from a clean cereal carton.
A length of soft wool.
A sheet of tissue paper.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish craft methods by the actions used to shape or join materials.
questions.prompt: Amaka presses a thumb into a ball of soft clay to open a hollow. Tunde joins two cardboard panels with a folded tab and glue. Name each craft method and explain how each action gives the object its shape.
questions.answer: Amaka is modelling or moulding: she presses and reshapes the clay. Tunde is constructing: he joins separate pieces to form a structure.
questions.explanation: Modelling changes the shape of a pliable material. Constructing builds a form by joining parts.

markingGuide.description: Names Amaka’s method as modelling or moulding.
Explains that pressure reshapes the clay to form a hollow.
Names Tunde’s method as constructing.
Explains that the tab joins separate parts to build the form.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of interlacing in a woven structure.
questions.prompt: At a classroom display, a pupil lays yellow paper strips across blue strips. The yellow strips lift away together when the display is tilted. Which change makes the strips interlace?
questions.answer: Pass each yellow strip above some blue strips and below others.
questions.explanation: An interlaced strip changes sides relative to the strips it crosses. Laying it on top of every crossing leaves the two sets separate.
options: Pass each yellow strip above some blue strips and below others.
Turn the display so the blue strips run left to right.
Trim the yellow strips so they all have equal length.
Align the ends of the blue strips along the edge of the table.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify plain and twill structures from the pattern of crossings.
questions.prompt: Swatch P alternates over one and under one, reversing on the next row. Swatch Q repeats over two and under two, shifting the repeat by one strand in each new row to form diagonal lines. Identify the weave in each swatch and use a visible clue from each to justify your choices.
questions.answer: P is plain weave because each crossing alternates and the next row reverses it. Q is a twill weave because the shift in each row produces diagonal lines.
questions.explanation: Plain weave uses alternating crossings. A stepped shift of the same repeat across consecutive rows is characteristic of twill.

markingGuide.description: Identifies P as plain weave.
Uses the alternating crossings or reversal in the next row as evidence.
Identifies Q as twill.
Connects the row shift or diagonal lines to twill.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Select weaving materials based on flexibility and strength.
questions.prompt: For a first hand-weaving exercise, a teacher has clean strips of locally available material. Which property matters most when the strips must pass repeatedly over and under each other?
questions.answer: They bend at crossings and stay intact.
questions.explanation: Strips need enough flexibility to change direction at crossings and enough strength to survive handling.
options: They make a sound when dropped.
They all have the same printed design.
They are stiff enough to snap at a tight bend.
They bend at crossings and stay intact.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Produce a handwoven object using available materials.
questions.prompt: Use the teacher’s prepared card base with at least five parallel strands joined at both ends, plus contrasting clean paper strips. Weave a flat bookmark using plain weave. Show the teacher how two adjacent rows differ before securing loose ends with paper tape.
questions.answer: An example alternates over and under in the first row. The second row begins under and reverses every crossing from row one. The remaining rows alternate the same way and the loose ends are taped.
questions.explanation: Opposite crossings in adjacent rows form the plain-weave structure. Securing the ends keeps the finished bookmark intact.

markingGuide.description: Interlaces the strips through the prepared base.
Alternates over and under consistently within a row.
Demonstrates opposite crossings in adjacent rows.
Secures ends and produces a flat bookmark.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Explain how attached fragments can be arranged to create a collage.
questions.prompt: A pupil is making a collage of a keke waiting in front of a kiosk. Which sequence best shows that the keke is nearer to the viewer?
questions.answer: Attach the kiosk shape first, then overlap a lower part of it with the keke shape.
questions.explanation: The shape covering part of another shape appears in front. Placing the keke on top makes the overlap support the intended depth.
options: Attach the keke shape first and cover part of it with the kiosk shape.
Place the two shapes far apart without any overlap.
Attach the kiosk shape first, then overlap a lower part of it with the keke shape.
Cover both shapes with one sheet of opaque card.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Select appropriate materials and tools for a collage.
questions.prompt: A pupil wants to add a piece of cotton fabric to a collage on thick card. A glue stick holds the paper pieces but the fabric corners lift. The teacher provides water-based craft glue, a scrap of card and a spreader. Describe how to test and attach the fabric with the new materials.
questions.answer: Test a thin layer of glue on a small fabric offcut and scrap card. Let it dry and see whether the edges hold and whether glue shows through. If the test works, spread a thin layer to the edges of the final piece and press it flat on the backing.
questions.explanation: Fabric can absorb glue and show stains. A small test checks the bond and appearance before the final piece is fixed.

markingGuide.description: Tests on an offcut and scrap backing.
Uses the spreader to apply a thin layer.
Lets the test dry and checks adhesion or visible staining.
Explains pressing down the final piece including its edges after a successful test.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Create a collage using attached materials with distinct surface qualities.
questions.prompt: On card, create a collage of a market stall. Use at least two of the supplied paper and fabric textures. Arrange the pieces before gluing, include a deliberate overlap and explain one choice of texture to the teacher.
questions.answer: For example, place smooth paper behind a rough fabric awning and overlap the awning with a paper sign. The rough fabric suggests the weave of a cloth canopy.
questions.explanation: Texture can suggest what an object is made from. Planning the overlap before gluing lets the artist decide which part appears in front.

markingGuide.description: Arranges distinct pieces to show a recognisable stall.
Uses two distinct textures.
Creates a deliberate overlap and fixes the pieces to the backing.
Explains how a texture helps depict part of the stall.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Identify how individual tesserae form a mosaic image.
questions.prompt: A school entrance sign shows a flower made of small ceramic pieces. No individual piece is shaped like a petal. What makes the flower visible?
questions.answer: The pieces work together through their colours and positions.
questions.explanation: A mosaic image emerges from the placement of separate units called tesserae. A group of pieces can define a petal or an outline.
options: The grout always changes colour to match a drawing.
Each piece must display the complete flower.
The pieces work together through their colours and positions.
The backing must already be shaped like a flower.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Describe the direct method of making a mosaic.
questions.prompt: A pupil has pre-cut paper tesserae and wants to model the direct method for a sign. Explain where the pieces are attached and when to check that the planned letter is readable.
questions.answer: Lay out the pieces over the letter guide on the backing and check that the letter is readable. Adjust as needed, then fix the pieces face up directly to that same backing.
questions.explanation: In the direct method the visible pieces are fixed to their final support. Testing the arrangement before attaching it lets the pupil adjust the outline and spacing.

markingGuide.description: Places the pieces on the intended final backing.
Checks readability before fixing.
Describes adjusting the arrangement if necessary.
Fixes the pieces face up directly on the final support.

questions.subject: Cultural and Creative Arts
questions.learningObjective: Draw an object and build a mosaic of it using separate units.
questions.prompt: Sketch a simple fish outline on card. Using the teacher’s pre-cut paper pieces in two contrasting colours, build a mosaic inside the outline. Use separate visible pieces for the body and for one detail, such as an eye or fin. Fix the pieces directly to the card.
questions.answer: One possible design uses yellow pieces for the body and dark blue pieces for the fin. The pieces follow the sketch, remain individually visible and are glued face up on the card.
questions.explanation: The sketch guides placement. Contrast makes a detail visible while the arrangement of separate pieces creates the overall fish shape.

markingGuide.description: Makes a recognisable outline before placing pieces.
Uses separate visible pieces to form the body.
Distinguishes a detail by contrasting colour.
Fixes pieces directly to the card and preserves the overall shape.
